title: Web and data security
scopeHtml:
Scope: TLS, OWASP top 10 for designers, secrets management, encryption at rest and in transit, key rotation.

Scope: TLS, OWASP top 10 for designers, secrets management, encryption at rest and in transit, key rotation.

notes.title: Threat modelling first
notes.html:
Security design starts by asking "who would attack this, what do they want, and how would they get in?" Without that you bolt on random controls.

Mechanism: draw the data-flow diagram, mark trust boundaries (internet to edge, edge to services, service to DB, your cloud to a third party), and run STRIDE on each crossing: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. Rank by impact times likelihood, then pick controls. Assume breach: any single layer will fail, so layer defences (defence in depth) and give each component least privilege.

Worked example. Payments app: crown jewels are card data and user PII. Threats: stolen DB backup (encrypt at rest, keys in KMS), SQL injection (parameterised queries, least-privilege DB user), insider reading rows (audit log, column encryption), DDoS (CDN, rate limit). Four threats, four controls, owners assigned.

Industry examples. Microsoft invented STRIDE; Stripe keeps card numbers in a small isolated vault so most services never see them (shrinking PCI scope); Google's BeyondCorp assumes the internal network is hostile.

Decision gravity. Threat modelling is cheap early and extremely expensive after launch. Choosing to keep sensitive data out of most services (tokenisation) is a one-way door in your favour.

Everyday analogy. Planning a house's security: doors, windows, a safe for jewellery, a dog, and a neighbour who watches. You do not rely on one lock.

Common interview traps.

  • Listing tools (WAF, TLS) without naming the threat each addresses.
  • Forgetting insiders and third-party dependencies.

notes.title: TLS: encryption in transit
notes.html:
TLS makes a connection private (nobody can read it), authentic (you talk to the real server) and tamper-proof. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.

Mechanism (TLS 1.3, 1 round trip): client sends ClientHello with supported ciphers and a key share (ECDHE); server replies with its key share, its certificate (public key signed by a CA) and a signature proving it holds the private key; both derive session keys; bulk data then uses AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. Forward secrecy: session keys are ephemeral, so stealing the server's private key later does not decrypt recorded traffic. TLS 1.3 resumption (0-RTT) saves a round trip but 0-RTT data can be replayed, so use it only for idempotent requests.

# nginx
ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/acme.crt;
ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/acme.key;
add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;
ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:50m;   # about 200k sessions

Worked example. A 100 ms RTT user: TCP handshake 100 ms + TLS 1.2 (2 RTT) 200 ms = 300 ms before the first byte; TLS 1.3 = 200 ms; with session resumption and a CDN edge terminating at 10 ms RTT, it drops to about 30 ms. Crypto CPU on modern hardware (AES-NI) is under 1% of a request, so "TLS is slow" is a myth.

Industry examples. Let's Encrypt issues free 90-day certificates (about 300M sites); Cloudflare and AWS ALB/CloudFront terminate TLS at the edge; Google enforces HTTPS via HSTS preload.

Decision gravity. Terminate at the edge and re-encrypt inside (or use mTLS) is easy to change. Dropping internal encryption "because it is a private network" is a decision attackers exploit after one foothold (NSA/Google SSL-added-and-removed-here incident).

Everyday analogy. Passing sealed, tamper-evident envelopes through a courier, after checking the recipient's ID with a notary (the CA).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying TLS protects data at rest.
  • Forgetting certificate expiry monitoring (outages at Microsoft Teams, Spotify and Equifax were expired certificates).
  • Not mentioning HSTS (stops downgrade to HTTP).

notes.title: mTLS and service-to-service security
notes.html:
Mutual TLS means both sides present certificates, so each service proves who it is. Inside a cluster this replaces "anyone on the network is trusted".

Mechanism: a private CA (or SPIFFE/SPIRE, Istio's Citadel, Linkerd identity) issues each workload a short-lived certificate (for example 24 h) naming its identity spiffe://prod/ns/payments/sa/api. The sidecar proxy or library does the handshake, so app code is unchanged. Authorisation policies then say "only orders may call payments".

# Istio: require mTLS in a namespace
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata: {name: default, namespace: prod}
spec: {mtls: {mode: STRICT}}

Worked example. 500 services, certs rotated every 24 h: 500 renewals/day, trivial for the CA, and a stolen cert is useless after a day. Handshake overhead is amortised by long-lived connections (HTTP/2 or gRPC).

Industry examples. Google ALTS, Lyft/Envoy, Netflix, Istio, Linkerd and AWS App Mesh. Zero-trust architectures (BeyondCorp) use the same idea for users.

Decision gravity. Starting with permissive mode, then moving to strict, is the safe path. Doing it late means a long migration.

Everyday analogy. Both people at the door show ID, not just the visitor.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing mTLS (who is calling) with user authorisation (what the user may do).
  • Long-lived certs that are never rotated.

notes.title: OWASP Top 10 for designers
notes.html:
The OWASP Top 10 lists the most common web flaws; designers should know the design-level cause and the structural fix of each. (2021 list; confirm for newer editions.)

# Risk Design-level fix
A01 Broken access control Deny by default, central authz, object-level checks
A02 Cryptographic failures TLS everywhere, strong algorithms, no secrets in code
A03 Injection (SQL, NoSQL, command, XSS) Parameterised queries, output encoding, CSP
A04 Insecure design Threat model, abuse cases, rate limits
A05 Security misconfiguration Hardened images, IaC scanning, no default creds
A06 Vulnerable components SBOM, dependency scanning, patch SLAs
A07 Identification and auth failures MFA, rate limit, secure sessions
A08 Software and data integrity failures Signed artifacts, CI/CD protection, no unsafe deserialisation
A09 Logging and monitoring failures Audit logs, alerting
A10 SSRF Egress allowlist, block metadata IPs 
// vulnerable
stmt.executeQuery("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + name + "'");
// safe
PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?");
ps.setString(1, name);

Worked example. SSRF: an image-URL fetcher lets an attacker request http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/, which returns cloud credentials. Fix: block link-local and private ranges, use IMDSv2 (token required), egress through a proxy with an allowlist, and give the instance a minimal IAM role.

Industry examples. Capital One 2019 breach combined SSRF, a misconfigured WAF and an over-privileged role (100M records). Log4Shell (2021, A06) hit almost every Java shop. Equifax 2017 was an unpatched Struts library.

Decision gravity. Parameterised queries and framework output encoding are free and should be non-negotiable. Retrofitting access-control checks across 200 endpoints is expensive; do it via middleware from the start.

Everyday analogy. A pre-flight checklist: every item exists because a plane once crashed for lack of it.

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting the list without a fix for each.
  • Thinking a WAF replaces secure code (it is a speed bump, not a wall).
  • Forgetting XSS and CSRF defences for cookie-based apps (CSP, SameSite, CSRF tokens).

notes.title: Secrets management
notes.html:
A secret is any credential (DB password, API key, signing key). Keep it out of code, images and logs, and fetch it at runtime from a dedicated store.

Mechanism: a secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, K8s secrets backed by KMS or External Secrets Operator) stores values encrypted, enforces IAM per secret, logs every access, and supports versions and rotation. Apps authenticate with their workload identity (IAM role, K8s service account), not with another static secret (avoids the "secret zero" problem). Prefer dynamic secrets: Vault creates a DB user valid for 1 h per request and drops it.

# Vault dynamic Postgres creds (lease 1h)
vault read database/creds/orders-ro
# username v-orders-ro-8fj2  password A1a-...  lease_duration 1h
# CI hygiene
gitleaks detect --source . ; git log -p | grep -i 'AKIA'

Worked example. 300 services x average 3 secrets = 900 secrets. Static secrets rotated quarterly = 3,600 rotations/year, impossible by hand, so automate. Dynamic secrets: leak window shrinks from months to 1 hour.

Industry examples. Uber (2016) lost AWS keys committed to a private GitHub repo (57M accounts); Toyota and others leaked keys in public repos for years. Netflix, Airbnb and Stripe use Vault-style systems with per-service identity.

Decision gravity. Introducing a secrets manager is cheap early. Rotating a secret baked into 40 deployed apps is a one-way, painful migration. Plan for rotation (apps must reload or support two valid versions).

Everyday analogy. A hotel safe with a log: staff get the combination for one shift only, instead of writing it on the wall.

Common interview traps.

  • Env vars in the image or docker inspect / crash dumps exposing them; mounted files or runtime fetch are better.
  • Committing .env files; deleting the commit does not remove the leak (rotate it).
  • Same secret across dev and prod.

notes.title: Encryption at rest
notes.html:
Encryption at rest protects stored data if disks, snapshots or backups are stolen. It does not stop a logged-in attacker or a SQL injection, because the DB decrypts for them.

Layers, from broad to fine:

  1. Full-disk / volume (EBS, LUKS, BitLocker): transparent, near-zero cost (AES-NI), covers lost disks.
  2. Database TDE (Postgres via disk or extensions, SQL Server/Oracle TDE, RDS storage encryption).
  3. Application-level / field-level: the app encrypts specific columns (card number, SSN) before writing; the DB and its admins see ciphertext only.

Envelope encryption is the pattern: a data key (DEK) encrypts the data (AES-256-GCM); a key encryption key (KEK) in KMS/HSM encrypts the DEK; you store the encrypted DEK next to the data. KMS is called only to unwrap DEKs, so you can re-key by re-wrapping tiny DEKs rather than re-encrypting terabytes.

# envelope sketch (AWS)
dk = kms.generate_data_key(KeyId="alias/orders", KeySpec="AES_256")
ct = AESGCM(dk["Plaintext"]).encrypt(nonce, plaintext, aad)   # unique nonce every time
store(ct, nonce, dk["CiphertextBlob"])   # wrapped DEK stored with the data

Worked example. 10 TB of S3 objects with one DEK per object: re-keying the KEK touches 10M small wrapped DEKs (minutes), not 10 TB of data (days). KMS costs about $0.03 per 10,000 requests, so cache DEKs in memory for a few minutes at 5k requests/s.

Industry examples. S3 SSE-KMS, RDS and EBS encryption, Google Tink library, Stripe encrypting card data with per-record keys in an HSM-backed vault, MongoDB Client-Side Field Level Encryption.

Decision gravity. Disk-level is a free default (turn it on at creation; enabling later may require a copy). Field-level encryption is a heavy one-way door: you lose indexing and search on those columns (use deterministic encryption or blind indexes, with trade-offs).

Everyday analogy. Locking your valuables in a box and putting the box key in the bank vault; to change the lock you swap the box key, not move all the valuables.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming "encrypted at rest" protects against app-level breaches.
  • Reusing a GCM nonce (breaks security catastrophically).
  • Storing the key next to the data.

notes.title: Encryption in transit vs at rest
notes.html:
In transit protects data moving between machines (TLS, mTLS, VPN, SSH); at rest protects stored bytes; "in use" (memory) is covered by enclaves. You need both because each covers a different attacker.

Hop Control
Browser to edge TLS 1.3, HSTS
Edge to service TLS re-encrypt or mTLS
Service to DB TLS (sslmode=verify-full in Postgres)
Service to Kafka TLS + SASL/mTLS listeners
Disk, backups, snapshots Volume or object encryption with KMS
Hot fields Field-level encryption
End-to-end Client-held keys (Signal, WhatsApp)

End-to-end encryption (E2EE): only the endpoints hold keys, the server sees ciphertext. WhatsApp and Signal use the Signal protocol (X3DH key agreement + Double Ratchet, giving forward secrecy per message). Trade-off: the server cannot search, moderate, or restore history without client-side help; multi-device and group chats need key distribution design.

Worked example. A Kafka cluster with TLS on every listener: CPU overhead is typically 10 to 30%, and zero-copy sendfile is lost for consumer fetches. Plan capacity with this in mind (confirm for your version and hardware).

Industry examples. Postgres sslmode=verify-full, Redis 6+ TLS, Kafka SSL listeners, Cloudflare Keyless SSL (private key stays in the customer's HSM).

Decision gravity. TLS everywhere is reversible config; E2EE is a one-way product decision because it prevents server-side features forever.

Everyday analogy. Armoured van for the road (in transit), vault in the bank (at rest), and a sealed letter only the recipient can open (E2EE).

Common interview traps.

  • Using sslmode=require (no certificate verification) and thinking it is safe from man-in-the-middle.
  • Forgetting backups, logs and analytics copies; they carry the same data.

notes.title: Key management and rotation
notes.html:
Keys must be generated, stored, used, rotated and destroyed with controls; the key is the real secret, not the algorithm.

Mechanism: keep root keys in an HSM or cloud KMS (keys never leave, you send data to be encrypted or wrapped). Separate keys by purpose and tenant (signing vs encryption; one KEK per environment or customer). Rotation limits the amount of data under one key and the damage of a leak:

  • KEK rotation (cheap): new KMS key version; new wraps use it; old versions remain for decrypt (AWS can auto-rotate yearly; re-wrap lazily).
  • DEK rotation: re-encrypt data in the background, or use per-object keys that age out.
  • Signing key rotation (JWT/JWKS): publish both old and new public keys by kid, start signing with the new, keep old for at least one token lifetime, then remove.
  • Compromise rotation is urgent: revoke, re-issue, re-encrypt, then investigate.
day 0   JWKS: [k1]        sign with k1
day 30  JWKS: [k1, k2]    sign with k2  (gateways pick up k2 via cache TTL 1h)
day 31  JWKS: [k2]        k1 tokens (15 min TTL) all expired

Worked example. AES-GCM with random 96-bit nonces is safe for about 2^32 (4 billion) messages per key; at 10k encryptions/s a key lasts about 5 days before you should rotate, which is why per-object DEKs or key-per-day schemes are used.

Industry examples. AWS KMS (FIPS 140-2 HSMs, automatic rotation), Google Cloud KMS, HashiCorp Vault transit engine ("encryption as a service"), Let's Encrypt automating 90-day cert rotation, Microsoft's 2023 Storm-0558 incident (a stolen signing key minted tokens).

Decision gravity. Design rotation in from day one: encrypted blobs should store a key version id. Without that, rotation becomes a risky one-way migration.

Everyday analogy. Changing the locks on a building on a schedule, and keeping a ring of old keys for rooms you have not yet re-keyed.

Common interview traps.

  • Rotating a key by deleting the old one (data becomes unreadable).
  • No overlap window, so valid tokens suddenly fail verification.
  • Same key for signing and encryption.

notes.title: Web hardening checklist
notes.html:
A few headers and habits close many holes cheaply.

  • CORS: allow only specific origins; never * with credentials.
  • CSP: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self' limits XSS impact.
  • Cookies: HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax.
  • Input: validate on the server (type, length, allowlist), encode on output, parameterise queries.
  • File uploads: random names, size cap, content-type sniffing, store outside web root (S3 with private ACL and pre-signed URLs), virus scan.
  • Dependencies: Dependabot/Renovate, npm audit, SBOM, pinned base images.
  • Least privilege: DB user for the app has no DROP; IAM roles scoped per service.
  • Errors: no stack traces to clients; log full detail internally.
  • Logging: never log passwords, tokens, card numbers or full PII; add request IDs.
add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff always;
add_header X-Frame-Options DENY always;
add_header Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'" always;
add_header Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin always;

Worked example. Upload of a 2 GB video: instead of proxying through your app (ties up a worker for minutes), issue a pre-signed S3 PUT URL valid 10 min, with a size and content-type condition; client uploads direct to S3; an event triggers scanning and processing.

Industry examples. Slack, GitHub and Google ship strict CSP; Mozilla Observatory grades sites on these headers; pre-signed URLs are used by Dropbox-style and Instagram-style upload paths.

Decision gravity. All reversible config, cheap, and high value; skipping them is the common failure, not misjudging them.

Everyday analogy. Locking the windows and not leaving a spare key under the mat: boring, effective.

Common interview traps.

  • CORS treated as a security boundary for servers (it only controls browsers).
  • Logging full request bodies "for debugging".

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Threat model first (STRIDE, trust boundaries); layer defences and use least privilege.
  • TLS 1.3 gives privacy, authenticity, integrity and forward secrecy; terminate at the edge but re-encrypt inside, and use mTLS between services with short-lived certs.
  • Know OWASP Top 10 with a design fix each: deny-by-default authz, parameterised queries, patched dependencies, SSRF egress controls, audit logging.
  • Secrets live in a secrets manager with workload identity; prefer dynamic short-lived secrets; leaked secrets must be rotated, not just deleted.
  • Encryption at rest uses envelope encryption (DEK wrapped by a KMS KEK); disk-level is a free default, field-level is a heavy trade-off; protects stolen media, not app breaches.
  • Rotate keys by versioning (store key id with the blob), overlap old and new, and never delete a key that still has data under it.
  • Harden basics: HSTS, CSP, cookie flags, strict CORS, safe uploads with pre-signed URLs, no secrets or PII in logs.

questions.promptHtml: In a design interview, how do you do threat modelling, and why before picking controls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors choose controls from threats, not from a checklist.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I draw the data flow, mark trust boundaries, list assets (what an attacker wants), then walk STRIDE (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege) at each boundary, rank by likelihood times impact and only then choose controls. Spending effort follows the risk, not the fashion.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Browser --(TLS)--> CDN/WAF --> API gateway --> Order svc --> DB
   ^ untrusted          ^ boundary          ^ boundary        ^ boundary
  • Assets: PII, payment tokens, credentials, availability of checkout.
  • At each crossing ask STRIDE: can someone spoof the caller (authn), tamper in transit (TLS/signing), read data (encryption, authz), flood (rate limit), escalate (least privilege)?
  • Output is a short list: threat, control, owner, residual risk. Example: "stolen DB backup -> encrypt at rest with KMS key, restrict restore role".
  • Do it early: adding mTLS or per-tenant keys later is a one-way-door pain.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Listing controls (WAF, MFA) with no named threat.
  • Only external attackers; ignoring insiders, leaked credentials and supply chain.
  • Doing it once and never revisiting after design changes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Biggest risks for a payments API? -> Broken authz, credential theft, replay, fraud, key compromise.
  2. How do you rank? -> Likelihood x impact, plus cost of the control and reversibility.
  3. How do you keep it alive? -> Review at each design doc and a security checklist in the PR template.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use HTTPS and hash passwords". Senior: trust boundaries, assets, ranked threats, owners and residual risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team encrypted everything in transit but let the support tool read all customer rows; the threat they missed was an insider with a valid login.

questions.promptHtml: What does TLS provide and how does the handshake work at a high level? Where do you terminate it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: TLS is everywhere; seniors know what it guarantees and where it ends.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: TLS gives confidentiality, integrity and server authentication (and optionally client authentication). The client and server agree on a cipher, the server proves identity with a certificate chained to a trusted CA, they derive a shared session key with ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (forward secrecy), then use fast symmetric encryption. I usually terminate at the edge load balancer and re-encrypt inside for sensitive traffic.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Client                         Server
ClientHello (versions, ciphers, SNI) ->
            <- ServerHello + certificate + key share
verify chain, hostname, expiry
key exchange (ECDHE) => session keys
Finished <->  Finished
encrypted application data (AES-GCM / ChaCha20)
  • TLS 1.3 needs one round trip (0-RTT resumption possible but replayable, use only for idempotent requests).
  • Cost: handshake is asymmetric crypto (about 1 ms CPU class); session resumption and keepalive avoid repeating it.
  • Termination point: at the LB gives one place to manage certs and enable L7 routing, but traffic behind it is plaintext unless re-encrypted. Zero-trust designs use TLS or mTLS hop by hop.
  • Certificates expire: 90 days with automation (ACME) is the norm.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking TLS protects data at rest, or that it hides who you talk to (SNI, IPs visible).
  • Disabling cert verification "temporarily" in a client.
  • Manual cert renewals.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is forward secrecy? -> Ephemeral keys per session, so a later key theft cannot decrypt recorded traffic.
  2. What is HSTS? -> Header telling browsers to use only HTTPS for a period.
  3. Why TLS 1.3 over 1.2? -> Fewer round trips, removes weak ciphers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "HTTPS encrypts traffic". Senior: handshake steps, termination trade-offs, cert automation, resumption and 0-RTT replay risks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Expired certificates remain one of the most common avoidable outages.

questions.contextHtml:
Saturday 03:12. Your public API (6k rps) returns errors for mobile clients, while the web app seems fine. Logs and a client trace:

mobile: javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException: PKIX path validation failed: certificate expired
$ echo | openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates
notBefore=Aug 15 00:00:00 2025 GMT
notAfter =Nov 13 00:00:00 2025 GMT

Web browsers work because the CDN serves a different, auto-renewed cert. The API hostname bypasses the CDN and uses a cert renewed by hand 90 days ago by an engineer who left.
questions.promptHtml: Mitigate, find root cause and prevent recurrence.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Renews the cert and goes back to bed; no automation, no monitoring, and does not ask why web was fine.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which hostnames and endpoints terminate where? Does the mobile app pin the cert? Is the issuing flow automated anywhere?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Issue a new cert (ACME or CA portal), deploy to the LB, reload. If the app pins the leaf cert it will keep failing; check before celebrating.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) expired leaf on the API listener (confirmed by the dates); (2) intermediate chain missing in the new cert (check after renewal); (3) client clock skew (red herring, many devices affected).
  4. How I'd verify: openssl s_client -showcerts for the full chain, SSL Labs or curl -v, test from a mobile build, watch error rate fall.
  5. Root cause: Two cert paths, one manual and undocumented; no expiry alert.
  6. Fix: Short term: renew and deploy. Long term: ACME automation (cert-manager, LB-managed certs), 60-day renewals, one path for all hostnames.
  7. Prevention: Alert at 30, 14 and 7 days from a probe that reads the cert from outside (not from the config), an inventory of all certs, pin to the public key or an intermediate with a backup pin, not the leaf.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Shorter lifetimes demand reliable automation; that is the point. I would not extend by buying a multi-year cert; the limits are shrinking.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Pinning shipped in the app? -> Ship a new version with backup pins; until then use the same key pair for renewal (CSR from the same key, verify).
  • How do you test the alert? -> Run a canary hostname with a 7-day cert.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An internal service-to-service cert expired at midnight on a holiday; the inventory had no entry because it was created by a script from a previous quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Renews only.
  • Hire: Explains the split path and adds alerts.
  • Strong hire: Handles pinning, chain checks, external probes and full automation.

questions.contextHtml:
A secret scanner flags that an AWS access key and a Stripe live key were committed to a public GitHub repo 41 minutes ago by an intern in config/prod.env. The key belongs to a service role with S3 read/write on the customer-uploads bucket. CloudTrail already shows:

10:42:11 GetCallerIdentity src=203.0.113.50  (unfamiliar IP)
10:42:40 ListBuckets
10:43:02 ListObjectsV2 bucket=prod-customer-uploads
10:44:15 GetObject x 18,200 over 6 minutes
questions.promptHtml: What do you do in the first hour and what changes after?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Deletes the file or force-pushes a history rewrite and considers it solved. The secret is already harvested.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which permissions does the key have? Is it long-lived? Which other systems share it? Is S3 data access logging on?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revoke (deactivate then delete) the AWS key and roll the Stripe key now, before cleanup. Attach a deny-all inline policy to the role as an extra stop. Open an incident, preserve CloudTrail and S3 access logs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) automated scrapers harvest GitHub within minutes (matches 90 seconds after push); (2) the same key exists elsewhere (CI, laptops); (3) the exfil already finished (18,200 objects).
  4. How I'd verify: CloudTrail/S3 data events for the key id, list of objects read, Athena over logs, search the org for the key string.
  5. Root cause: Static long-lived credentials in a file, no pre-commit scanning, over-broad role.
  6. Fix: Short term as above, then scope exposure for notification (which customer files), rotate dependent secrets. Long term: no static keys: workload identity (IAM roles, OIDC to the cloud), a secrets manager with short leases, least-privilege per-service roles, and push protection.
  7. Prevention: Pre-commit and server-side secret scanning (push protection), .env in gitignore templates, anomaly alerts on GetObject volume, separate buckets with narrow policies.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rewrite git history first (secret still valid and cloned); history cleanup is hygiene after rotation. Do not blame the intern; the system allowed it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Key was in a private repo? -> Still rotate; the blast radius is anyone with read access and every clone.
  • How do you rotate without downtime? -> Create the new key, deploy, then delete the old.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A key leaked for 11 minutes and was used to mine crypto for a weekend because the cloud account had no spend alert.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Deletes the commit.
  • Hire: Rotates first, checks logs.
  • Strong hire: Scopes exposure, notifies, removes static credentials structurally and adds detection.

questions.contextHtml:
Review of a user-profile update endpoint:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@PutMapping("/users/{id}")
public User update(@PathVariable long id, @RequestBody User body) {
    String sql = "UPDATE users SET name='" + body.getName() + "' WHERE id=" + id;
    jdbc.execute(sql);
    userRepo.save(body);              // User has fields: id, name, email, role, isAdmin
    return body;
}
@PutMapping("/users/{id}")
fun update(@PathVariable id: Long, @RequestBody body: User): User {
    jdbc.execute("UPDATE users SET name='${body.name}' WHERE id=$id")
    userRepo.save(body)               // User has: id, name, email, role, isAdmin
    return body
}
questions.promptHtml: Find every vulnerability, class it by OWASP category, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Finds the SQL injection only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who may call this (self or admin)? Which fields may change? What data does the response expose?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the endpoint or put a WAF rule as a stopgap; check logs for ' and isAdmin in bodies.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) SQL injection from string concatenation (injection); (2) mass assignment: client sets role and isAdmin (broken access control, privilege escalation); (3) IDOR: nothing verifies id equals the caller; (4) returning the entity may leak internal fields (excessive data exposure).
  4. How I'd verify: Send name = x' ; UPDATE users SET isAdmin=true --; send body with "isAdmin":true; call with another user's id.
  5. Root cause: Binding raw request bodies to the persistence entity and building SQL by hand, with no object-level authz.
  6. Fix: Use a request DTO with only name; parameterised statements or ORM; take the id from the authenticated principal; return a response DTO.
jdbc.update("UPDATE users SET name=? WHERE id=?", dto.name(), principal.userId());
  1. Prevention: Lint banning string-concatenated SQL, DTO convention, authz tests (user A updating user B), SAST in CI.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not "sanitize" the quote characters by hand; parameterisation is the fix. A WAF is a net, not a cure.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not blocklist words like DROP? -> Trivially bypassed, breaks legit data.
  • Does an ORM make you safe? -> Not if you concatenate into JPQL or native queries.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A PATCH endpoint accepted "tenantId" from the body; a tester moved their account into another customer's tenant.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: SQLi only.
  • Hire: SQLi, mass assignment, IDOR.
  • Strong hire: Adds DTOs, principal-derived id, tests and CI enforcement.

questions.promptHtml: Explain envelope encryption. How do you encrypt data at rest at scale, and what does it actually protect against?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "We encrypt at rest" is often a checkbox; the senior answer knows the threat model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each object or record is encrypted with a data key (DEK); the DEK is itself encrypted by a master key (KEK) held in a KMS/HSM. You store the wrapped DEK next to the ciphertext. This makes rotation and access control cheap and keeps the master key off the data path. Disk or database-level encryption protects against stolen disks and backups, not against a compromised app with valid credentials.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
write: DEK = random 256-bit; ciphertext = AES-GCM(DEK, data)
       wrapped = KMS.Encrypt(KEK, DEK)       -> store (wrapped, ciphertext)
read : DEK = KMS.Decrypt(wrapped)            -> decrypt
  • Layers: full-disk/volume (protects lost hardware), database TDE or S3 SSE (protects storage media and backups), application-level field encryption (protects against DB admins and SQL dumps; breaks search unless you add blind indexes).
  • KMS call cost: tens of ms and quota-limited (thousands of requests/s, verify per provider), so cache DEKs in memory for a short time.
  • Rotating the KEK only re-wraps small DEKs, never re-encrypts terabytes.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing the key next to the data, or in the same DB.
  • Believing TDE stops SQL injection (the DB decrypts for the query).
  • One global key for all tenants.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Per-tenant keys? -> Enables crypto-shredding for deletion and isolates breach; costs key management overhead.
  2. How do you search encrypted fields? -> Blind index (HMAC) for equality; range and fuzzy search need trade-offs.
  3. What if KMS is down? -> Cached DEKs keep reads going for the cache TTL; plan multi-region keys.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "AES-256 at rest". Senior: envelope scheme, layers vs threats, KMS quotas and caching, crypto-shredding.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team with TDE still leaked data by SQL injection because the database decrypted transparently for the attacker.

questions.contextHtml:
A pentest report on a SPA plus API lists these findings. Config excerpts:

Set-Cookie: session=9a8f...; Path=/
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true      (server reflects the Origin header in practice)
No Content-Security-Policy, no X-Frame-Options
POST /transfer works with a cookie and no CSRF token
JWT stored in localStorage
questions.promptHtml: Which are real risks, in what order do you fix them, and what is the target configuration?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds a header or two without understanding which attack each one blocks.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we use cookies for auth or bearer tokens? Which origins legitimately call the API? Any third-party scripts on the page?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the CORS reflection first: with credentials, a reflected origin lets any site read authenticated responses.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) CORS reflection with credentials: cross-site data theft; (2) cookie without HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite: stealable by XSS, sent cross-site (CSRF); (3) no CSRF defence on a state-changing POST; (4) no CSP: XSS has free rein; (5) clickjacking (no frame-ancestors); (6) token in localStorage: any XSS exfiltrates it.
  4. How I'd verify: Request from evil.test origin and confirm the reflected header; craft an auto-submitting form against /transfer; check cookie flags in devtools.
  5. Root cause: Defaults left on, security headers not part of the platform template.
  6. Fix:
Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=3600
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com   (explicit allowlist, Vary: Origin)
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

Add a CSRF token or rely on SameSite plus an Origin check for unsafe methods; keep tokens in HttpOnly cookies. 7. Prevention: Put headers in the gateway or framework middleware, run a header scanner in CI, review CSP in report-only mode first. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A strict CSP can break inline scripts; roll out with report-only. I would not use * anywhere credentials flow.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does SameSite replace CSRF tokens? -> Reduces most cases; keep tokens or Origin checks for defence in depth and legacy browsers.
  • Why HttpOnly if XSS can still act as the user? -> It stops token theft for later use, not in-page actions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A reflected-origin CORS bug exposed account pages to any visited site; fixing it was a five-line allowlist.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds headers randomly.
  • Hire: Prioritises CORS and cookie flags.
  • Strong hire: Explains each attack, rollout of CSP, CSRF strategy.

questions.contextHtml: 80 microservices in Kubernetes talk plain HTTP inside the cluster; peak 120k internal rps. A compliance audit requires encrypted and mutually authenticated service traffic within 6 months, without downtime. Some services are legacy and cannot be changed. You are evaluating a service mesh (sidecar mTLS) versus library-level TLS.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the rollout with numbers and failure modes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Turn on strict mTLS everywhere on Monday." Breaks anything not in the mesh and ignores cert rotation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which languages and which services cannot take a sidecar? What is the latency budget? Who runs the CA? Is there traffic leaving the cluster?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; this is a migration. I start with visibility: which service calls which (mesh telemetry in permissive mode).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (risks): (1) non-mesh clients break under strict mode; (2) sidecar adds latency and CPU (rough 1 to 3 ms per hop and 10 to 20% CPU, verify by load test); (3) cert expiry/rotation failure takes down traffic; (4) health probes and jobs fail.
  4. How I'd verify: Canary one namespace in permissive mode; compare p99 before and after; confirm all traffic shows mTLS in telemetry.
  5. Root cause (why mesh): Identity per workload (SPIFFE-style IDs), automated short-lived certs (for example 24 h) and policy "service A may call B" without app changes.
  6. Fix (plan): Phase 1 sidecar injection in permissive mode; Phase 2 strict mode namespace by namespace, starting with low-risk; Phase 3 authorization policies by service identity; exceptions get a gateway or an allowlist with an expiry date. Keep the CA root offline and intermediates in KMS/HSM.
  7. Prevention: Alert on cert-age and failed handshakes, game day where the CA is unavailable (existing certs keep working until expiry), dashboards of plaintext remaining.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The mesh gives uniform policy but adds operational weight and latency; library TLS has no sidecar but needs every language to manage certs. I would not make strict mode global at once, and not issue year-long certs to avoid rotation work.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cost? -> 80 services x 3 pods x 100 MB sidecar is about 24 GB RAM; budget it.
  • Does mTLS replace authz? -> No, it proves who is calling; policies decide what is allowed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Strict mode silently broke a nightly batch job outside the mesh; permissive-mode telemetry would have shown the caller.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Big-bang flip.
  • Hire: Permissive then strict, namespace by namespace.
  • Strong hire: Identity-based policy, cert lifecycle, exceptions with expiry, cost and latency numbers.

questions.contextHtml: A healthcare startup's enterprise customer writes: "All patient data must be encrypted." You run Postgres on managed cloud storage (500 GB), S3 for scans (20 TB), Kafka between services, and an analytics warehouse. The CTO wants the cheapest approach that passes the customer's security review in four weeks.
questions.promptHtml: How do you turn the vague requirement into a design, and what do you encrypt where?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Turn on AES-256 everywhere" with no threat model, key plan or cost view.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which regulations (HIPAA, GDPR)? Which threat: stolen disk, insider, breach, cloud operator? Does the customer require customer-managed keys? Is searchable data needed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Baseline in week one: confirm TLS 1.2+ on every hop and enable platform encryption (volumes, S3 SSE-KMS, Kafka TLS, warehouse), since these are config flags.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) the customer mostly needs in-transit plus at-rest baseline and key control evidence; (2) high-sensitivity fields (SSN, diagnosis) may need field-level encryption; (3) backups and logs are the usual gap.
  4. How I'd verify: Inventory every data store and hop; check backups, replicas, logs, analytics exports, developer laptops and test data.
  5. Root cause of ambiguity: Encryption is a control, not a requirement; the requirement is "what attack must fail".
  6. Fix (design): In transit: TLS everywhere, mTLS internally later. At rest: KMS-managed keys per environment (customer-managed key option for this customer), SSE-KMS on S3 with bucket policy denying unencrypted uploads, encrypted Postgres storage plus backups, field-level envelope encryption for the most sensitive columns. Redact PII from logs. Document the key hierarchy and access reviews as audit evidence.
  7. Prevention: IaC policies that fail builds for unencrypted resources, key-usage alerts, quarterly access review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Field-level encryption costs search and query flexibility; apply it to few columns. Per-customer keys add complexity (one-way door when you promise it to customers). I would not build custom crypto.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• KMS cost? -> Roughly $1 per key per month plus per-request charges (verify); cache DEKs.
  • Why not only disk encryption? -> It does not protect against a compromised app or a DBA.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The audit failed on an unencrypted analytics export bucket that no architecture diagram showed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Encrypt everything with AES-256".
  • Hire: In transit vs at rest layering with KMS.
  • Strong hire: Threat-driven, inventory including backups and logs, customer-managed keys and cost/complexity trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml:
After enabling application-level encryption, checkout latency p99 rises from 80 ms to 2.4 s at peak 9k rps. Logs:

ERROR KmsThrottlingException: Rate exceeded (ThrottlingException) region=eu-west-1
kms.Decrypt calls: 9,300/s   (account quota in this region: about 5,500/s shared - verify)
cache: none; each request decrypts a wrapped DEK
retry: 3 immediate retries, no jitter

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Asks for a quota increase and keeps the design.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Per-request or per-tenant DEKs? Can the DEK live in memory? Do other services share the KMS quota?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a short in-memory DEK cache (TTL 5 minutes, bounded size) behind a feature flag; stop immediate retries; request a quota increase in parallel.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) decrypt per request exceeds quota; (2) retry storm multiplies calls (no jitter, 3 retries makes 9k into up to 36k); (3) other workloads share the quota (check).
  4. How I'd verify: CloudWatch KMS metrics by key and caller, throttling counts, distinct DEKs per second; compare cache hit simulation.
  5. Root cause: Using KMS as a per-request crypto engine; it is meant to protect keys, with limited throughput.
  6. Fix: Envelope encryption with cached DEKs (for example one DEK per tenant per hour), exponential backoff with jitter, request coalescing (singleflight). With 20k distinct DEKs active, cache hit ratio is above 99% so KMS calls drop to tens per second.
SecretKey dek = cache.get(tenantId, t -> kms.decrypt(wrappedFor(t))); // Caffeine, expireAfterWrite 5 min
  1. Prevention: Load test with KMS rate limits modelled, alert at 60% of quota, per-service keys to isolate quotas.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Cached DEKs live in memory longer; accept it with short TTLs and no heap dumps in logs. I would not cache plaintext DEKs on disk or in Redis.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Region outage? -> Multi-Region keys and cached DEKs buy time; reads continue while cache lasts.
  • Rotation with a cache? -> KEK rotation re-wraps; cache entries just expire.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A retry loop with no jitter turned a small throttle into a 10x call storm that locked out every other team using the same account quota.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Raises quota only.
  • Hire: Caches DEKs.
  • Strong hire: Retry storm analysis, singleflight, quota isolation and security of cached keys.

questions.contextHtml:
A "fetch image from URL" feature in your profile service lets users paste an image URL; the server downloads it for resizing. GuardDuty alerts on unusual use of an instance role from an external IP. Request logs show:

POST /profile/avatar {"url":"http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/profile-svc-role"}
200 OK  (response body returned to caller in an error message)

The role has s3:* and dynamodb:* on production resources. IMDSv1 is enabled.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blocks the string 169.254. Easily bypassed with redirects, DNS rebinding and alternative encodings.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which role and permissions? Is IMDSv2 enforceable? What other internal services does this host reach? What did CloudTrail show for the stolen credentials?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the feature, rotate by revoking role sessions (attach a deny policy for tokens issued before now), review CloudTrail for the credential use, start incident response.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) SSRF to the metadata service returning role credentials; (2) other internal endpoints also reached (admin consoles, internal APIs); (3) credentials used from outside (GuardDuty says yes).
  4. How I'd verify: CloudTrail by access key id and source IP; egress logs; replay the request in a sandbox.
  5. Root cause: Server-side fetch of attacker-chosen URLs from a network position with metadata and internal reachability, plus an over-privileged role and IMDSv1.
  6. Fix: Enforce IMDSv2 with hop limit 1; narrow the role to the one bucket needed; fetch through an egress proxy in an isolated network that cannot reach internal ranges; allowlist schemes (https only), resolve DNS once, reject private, link-local and loopback ranges after resolution, do not follow redirects blindly, cap size and time, never return raw error bodies.
  7. Prevention: SAST rule for outbound fetch with user URLs, SSRF tests in pentests, least-privilege review, GuardDuty alerts routed to on-call.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: An isolated fetcher service adds a hop but contains the risk. I would not rely on a blocklist of hostnames.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• DNS rebinding? -> Resolve, validate, then connect to the validated IP directly.
  • Do webhooks have the same risk? -> Yes, same controls on the outbound sender.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A link-preview feature fetched URLs from the same network as the metadata service; the fix was moving fetches to a sandboxed worker pool with no credentials at all.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blocks a string.
  • Hire: Resolves and validates addresses, IMDSv2.
  • Strong hire: Isolated egress, least-privilege role, session revocation and detection.

questions.promptHtml: How do you design key management and rotation: for signing keys, data-encryption keys and the master key? What happens when a key is compromised?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Rotation is where crypto designs break in production; a senior has a plan before the compromise.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep a hierarchy: root keys in an HSM/KMS, key-encrypting keys below, data keys per object or tenant. Rotate on a schedule and on compromise, with versioned keys so old data stays readable. For signing keys, publish multiple public keys (JWKS with kid), overlap old and new for the token lifetime, then retire. For compromise, revoke, re-encrypt affected data and treat it as an incident, not a config change.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Root (HSM) -> KEK (KMS, rotates yearly, auto) -> DEK (per tenant/object, rotates on schedule)
Signing: kid=2026-01 (active)  kid=2025-07 (verify only, until tokens expire)
  • KEK rotation: new version wraps new DEKs; old versions remain to decrypt; re-wrap is cheap. Full re-encryption of data (rewriting terabytes) is only needed after compromise.
  • Signing key rotation: add new key to JWKS, wait for caches (a few minutes to an hour), switch issuing, keep the old for token TTL plus margin, then remove.
  • Compromise: revoke immediately, issue new keys, force token re-issue, re-encrypt data under a new key, investigate usage logs.
  • Never store keys in code or config; use IAM-bound access, audit every key use.
  • Numbers: re-encrypting 100 TB at 1 GB/s takes about 28 hours, so plan lazily (re-encrypt on write or by a background job with throttling).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No kid, so rotation breaks every verifier at once.
  • Rotating by deleting the old key (old data unreadable).
  • Rotating the KEK and believing the data was re-encrypted.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Crypto-shredding? -> Delete the tenant's key to make their data unrecoverable.
  2. How often to rotate? -> Policy-driven (for example yearly KEK, shorter for signing); automate so frequency is not a cost.
  3. Backup keys? -> Escrow with split knowledge and tested recovery; losing the key is data loss.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "rotate keys periodically". Senior: hierarchy, overlap windows, rewrap vs re-encrypt, compromise runbook, escrow and re-encryption time.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A rotation that removed the old signing key logged out every user at once because verifiers had no overlap window.
